question.text: The second-order differential equation \[ y'' + t y' - t^3y= e^{t} \] can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = f(t) \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t)$ and $x_2(t) = y'(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1(t) &= y \\[5pt] x_2(t) & = y'. \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1'(t) &= y' \\[5pt] x_2'(t) & = y'' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = y''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain \[ y'' = -t y' + t^3y + e^{t}. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y'' = -t x_2 + t^3x_1 + e^{t}. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = t^3x_1 -t x_2 + e^{t} \end{cases} \]

Finally,

\[ f(t) = t^3x_1 -t x_2 + e^{t}. \]

question.text: The second-order differential equation \[ y'' - 3t y' + t^2 y = 6 \] can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = f(t) \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t)$ and $x_2(t) = y'(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1(t) &= y \\[5pt] x_2(t) & = y' \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1'(t) &= y' \\[5pt] x_2'(t) & = y'' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = y''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain \[ y'' = 3t y' - t^2 y + 6. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y'' = 3t x_2 - t^2 x_1 + 6. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = -t^2 x_1 + 3t x_2 + 6 \end{cases} \]

Finally, \[ f(t) = -t^2 x_1 + 3t x_2 + 6. \]

question.text: The third-order differential equation \[ y''' - y'' + 3y' - \cos{t} \, y= 2t \] can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3\\[5pt] x_3' = f(t) \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t)$ and $x_3(t) = y''(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1(t) & = y \\[5pt] x_2(t) & = y'\\[5pt] x_3(t) & = y'' \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1'(t) & = y' \\[5pt] x_2'(t) & = y''\\[5pt] x_3'(t) & = y''' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = y'''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1,$ $x_2,$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain \[ y''' = y'' - 3y' + \cos{t} \, y + 2t. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y''' = x_3 - 3x_2 + \cos{t} \, x_1 + 2t. \]

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = \cos{t} \, x_1 - 3 x_2 + x_3 + 2t. \end{cases} \]

Finally, \[ f(t) = \cos{t} \, x_1 - 3 x_2 + x_3 + 2t. \]

question.text: The third-order differential equation \[ y''' - \sqrt{t}\,y'' - y= t^2 \] can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3\\[5pt] x_3' = f(t) \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t)$ and $x_3(t) = y''(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1(t) & = y \\[5pt] x_2(t) & = y'\\[5pt] x_3(t) & = y'' \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1'(t) & = y' \\[5pt] x_2'(t) & = y''\\[5pt] x_3'(t) & = y''' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = y'''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1,$ $x_2,$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain \[ y''' = \sqrt{t} \, y'' + y + t^2. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y''' = \sqrt{t} \, x_3 + x_1 + t^2. \]

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = x_1 + \sqrt{t} \, x_3 + t^2. \end{cases} \]

Finally, \[ f(t) = x_1 + \sqrt{t} \, x_3 + t^2. \]

question.text: The third-order differential equation \[ y''' + \dfrac{1}{t} \, y'' - t^2 y' = \dfrac{1}{t^2} \] can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3\\[5pt] x_3' = f(t) \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t)$ and $x_3(t) = y''(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1(t) & = y \\[5pt] x_2(t) & = y'\\[5pt] x_3(t) & = y'' \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1'(t) & = y' \\[5pt] x_2'(t) & = y''\\[5pt] x_3'(t) & = y''' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = y'''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1,$ $x_2,$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain \[ y''' = -\dfrac{1}{t} \, y'' + t^2 y' + \dfrac{1}{t^2}. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y''' = -\dfrac{1}{t} \, x_3 + t^2 x_2 + \dfrac{1}{t^2}. \]

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = t^2 x_2 - \dfrac{1}{t} \, x_3 + \dfrac{1}{t^2}. \end{cases} \]

Finally, \[ f(t) = t^2 x_2 - \dfrac{1}{t} \, x_3 + \dfrac{1}{t^2}. \]

question.explanation:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1 &= y \\[5pt] x_2 & = y'\\[5pt] x_3 & = y'' \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1' = y', \\[5pt] x_2' = y'',\\[5pt] x_3' = y''' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = y'''. \end{cases} \]

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1, x_2,$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain \[ y''' = -t^2 y'' + e^{2t} y' + \sin t. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y''' = -t^2 x_3 + e^{2t} x_2 + \sin t. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3 \\[5pt] x_3' = e^{2t} x_2 - t^2 x_3 + \sin t \end{cases} \]

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t) + \mathbf f(t)$ as follows: \[ \begin{bmatrix} x_1' \\ x_2'\\ x_3' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0}\\ 0 & 0 & \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{1}\\ 0 & e^{2t} & \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{-t^2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0}\\ \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\sin t} \end{bmatrix} \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y'' = -2x_2 - 3x_1 + e^{2t}. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = -3x_1 - 2x_2 + e^{2t} \end{cases} \]

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t) + \mathbf f(t)$ as follows: \[ \begin{bmatrix} x_1' \\ x_2' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0} & \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{1} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{-3} & \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{-2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{e^{2t}} \end{bmatrix} \]
